question: For graph connectivity, when can a finite-depth Transformer express matrix powering, and under what architecture, optimization, symmetry, and data-distribution conditions does training select that algorithm rather than a global degree shortcut?

key_findings.claim: A two-layer standard Transformer fits held-out Erdos-Renyi graphs while failing almost completely on simple same-size disconnected chains and cliques.
key_findings.evidence: The preliminary model is trained on ER(n=20,p=0.08) adjacency matrices and attains nearly perfect in-distribution exact match, yet its graph-level exact-match accuracy is near zero on 2Chain and 2Clique. The two chains have maximum within-component distance 9, exactly the paper's claimed 3^2 capacity, so the failure is not attributed to the constructive capacity bound.

key_findings.claim: The constructive expressivity result is exact for the paper's Disentangled Transformer: identity attention weights yield support equal to A^(3^L).
key_findings.evidence: With h0=[I|A], each layer appends (h h^T)h/n. Setting every W_l to identity triples the largest adjacency power available at each layer, and the all-block readout has support supp(A^(3^L)); self-loops make this equal connectivity for graphs whose maximum component diameter is at most 3^L.

key_findings.claim: The matching 3^L capacity upper bound is restricted to nonnegative Disentangled-Transformer weights and sufficiently many nodes.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.5 assumes every W_l is entrywise nonnegative and n >= (7/3)3^L+2. Its proof splits into an intermediate false-positive certificate construction and a no-false-positive locality induction; it does not prove the same upper bound for signed weights, softmax attention, or the standard Transformer used in experiments.

anchors.section: Appendix B.2, Theorem 4.5 and Lemma B.1
Appendix B.2, Locality proof and theorem conclusion

key_findings.claim: The paper's diameter convention is nonstandard and materially changes the meaning of within capacity for disconnected graphs.
key_findings.evidence: diam(G) is defined as the maximum finite diameter of any connected component rather than infinity for a disconnected graph. Thus a disconnected union of short components is within capacity even though ordinary all-pairs graph diameter would be infinite.

key_findings.claim: The Disentangled Transformer gains traceability by paying an exponential-width and nonstandard-attention cost.
key_findings.evidence: Its hidden dimension doubles each layer, d_l=2^(l+1)n; attention is unnormalized 1/n ReLU(hWh^T)h; outputs from attention are appended rather than added; and the readout sums all n-wide slices. The standard experimental model also replaces softmax with normalized ReLU attention, so neither route is an ordinary deployed Transformer specification.

anchors.section: Appendix A, Definition A.1 of the standard model

key_findings.claim: The algorithmic-versus-heuristic channel decomposition follows only from a strong layerwise equivariance assumption over arbitrary hidden states.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.7 proves W_l=A_l tensor I_n + B_l tensor J_n when nonnegative attention is equivariant for every feasible h and every permutation. Appendix C explicitly notes this is stronger than graph-induced equivariance; empirical cosine consistency and small projection error make the assumption plausible for tested runs but do not prove exact decomposition or functional necessity.

anchors.section: Appendix C.1, Theorem 4.7 and Remark C.3
Appendix C.1, Proof by weight conjugation

key_findings.claim: Within the equivariant algebra, the I channel is local matrix powering while the J channel broadcasts degree-derived global statistics.
key_findings.evidence: A tensor I_n preserves node-local structure and composes adjacency powers; B tensor J_n uses Jx=(1^T x)1 and AJ=d1^T, yielding degree products and higher-order global summaries. Such summaries correlate with connectivity in random graphs but make false connections between disconnected high-degree cliques.

key_findings.claim: The formal training-dynamics results do not prove the headline's simple rule that a majority of within-capacity examples makes Transformers learn the algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: Theorems C.5 and C.9 require nonnegative equivariant parameterization, a special exponential link and surrogate cross-entropy, activation conditions, B=0 for several per-sample claims, unsaturated pairs, and a quantitative cross-component-penalty dominance inequality. That weighted gradient condition depends on scores and sensitivities, not merely the count or majority of within-capacity graphs.

anchors.section: Appendix C.4, Per-sample proof and population mixture

key_findings.claim: Projected-gradient convergence is established only for a regularized population objective in the constrained decomposed parameter space, not for the AdamW training used in the principal experiments.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.9 studies full population risk with projection onto nonnegative A_l,B_l and L2 regularization. The appendix proves sufficient decrease and that limit points are KKT under a small step size; actual two- and three-layer experiments use AdamW from unrestricted random weights, while only the one-layer experiment uses full-batch standard gradient descent on a finite set.

anchors.section: Appendix C.5.2-5.3, Smoothness and sufficient decrease

key_findings.claim: The stated O(1/K) approximate-KKT rate is ambiguous: the proof bounds the squared gradient-mapping norm, not the norm itself.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 27 establishes min_k ||G_eta(Theta_k)||^2 <= constant/K, after which the text calls the iterate epsilon-approximate KKT with epsilon=O(1/K). Unless epsilon is explicitly defined as squared stationarity residual, the norm rate is O(K^-1/2), and the paper does not define the approximation convention.

key_findings.claim: The appendix does not prove its final claim that suppressing the J channel automatically reaches capacity 3^L.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary C.22 says B_l=0 implies the model reaches the tight capacity bound, citing Lemma C.12. But Lemma C.12 proves only Z_ij>0 implies [A^(3^L)]_ij>0—an upper-support/locality statement. It does not prove every reachable within-capacity pair gets positive output; for example, zero A-channel weights also satisfy B=0 but do not solve connectivity.

key_findings.claim: The regularized heuristic-suppression corollary is close to vacuous as written because its strict premise cannot hold at the claimed B=0 conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: Corollary C.20 defines D as the directional derivative along B*_l and assumes a strict penalty-over-reward inequality. If B*_l=0, that direction is zero and both sides of the strict inequality are zero; if B*_l is nonzero, the inequality contradicts KKT complementarity. The argument is useful as a contradiction test for nonzero B, but it does not identify when a realizable limit point satisfies the premise.

key_findings.claim: Empirical distance-threshold results are supportive but do not validate the exact theoretical capacity theorem for standard Transformers.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 2 and 10 report at least 99% pair accuracy up to distance 3^L and deterioration beyond it. The standard models use signed weights despite the theorem's nonnegativity assumption, and the metric is reliable pair accuracy rather than perfection on every graph required by Definition 4.4.

key_findings.claim: Capacity-filtered data improves selected OOD tests, but finite test panels and channel projections do not establish that the exact algorithm was learned.
key_findings.evidence: Restricting training to diam(G)<=3^L raises the projected I-channel energy and enables same-n 2Chain and 2Clique generalization. There is no exhaustive graph test, size extrapolation, causal channel ablation, or proof that another heuristic cannot pass those two families; energy share is a non-orthogonal Frobenius projection and can double-count overlap between I and J terms.

key_findings.claim: The data lever has a privileged-computation and distribution-confounding cost.
key_findings.evidence: Filtering or stratifying by graph diameter requires computing connected components and shortest-path diameter before training, which is closely related to the target structure. It also changes density, connectivity rates, distance mix, and negative-pair frequency, so experiments do not isolate capacity membership from all correlated graph statistics.

anchors.section: 5.2, Definition of G<=, G>, and stratified sampling

key_findings.claim: The negative result that overly easy data also fails is important and narrows the prescription beyond merely removing hard examples.
key_findings.evidence: For a one-layer capacity of 3, training only on graphs of diameter at most 2 fails to length-generalize to longer 2Chain cases, while admitting diameter-4 graphs promotes the J channel. Figure 12 indicates the best behavior when at-capacity diameter-3 examples are present and beyond-capacity examples are excluded.

key_findings.claim: The empirical scope is fixed-size synthetic adjacency prediction with unusually large data exposure, not general graph or language reasoning.
key_findings.evidence: The standard two-layer model has d=512 and is trained for 10^6 steps on one billion n=20 graphs; Disentangled two- and three-layer models likewise see one billion graphs at n=20 or 64. Inputs include the identity as node-position features and read-in/read-out dimensions depend on n, so the reported OOD tests change graph family but not input length.

method.core_idea: Use graph diameter to make Transformer algorithmic capacity exact, decompose permutation-equivariant Disentangled-Transformer weights into local matrix-powering and global degree-statistic channels, and manipulate the training distribution so gradient pressure favors the local channel.
method.mechanism: A self-loop-augmented adjacency matrix is fed to either a standard normalized-ReLU Transformer or a Disentangled Transformer that appends attention outputs. Identity weights construct adjacency powers through cubic composition. Under nonnegativity and strong layerwise permutation equivariance, weights decompose into A tensor I plus B tensor J. A surrogate population-loss analysis compares reward on connected pairs against penalties on disconnected cross-component pairs; synthetic experiments filter or stratify Erdos-Renyi graphs by diameter and assess same-size chain/clique OOD generalization.
assumptions: Graph inputs are finite, simple, undirected, self-loop augmented, and represented as dense n-by-n matrices with node identities as features.
Disentangled hidden width may grow exponentially with layer count and linearly with node count.
All theoretical attention weights and decomposed A/B parameters are entrywise nonnegative, making ReLU inactive on the relevant scores.
Layerwise permutation equivariance holds for every feasible nonnegative hidden state, not only states induced by graphs.
Training remains in the A tensor I plus B tensor J algebra and uses projected full-population gradient descent with a sufficiently small step size.
The exponential link surrogate, epsilon smoothing, L2 regularization, saturation conditions, and activation conditions represent the empirical objective.
Cross-component penalty dominates within-component reward at relevant stationary points.
Passing selected 2Chain and 2Clique OOD tests plus high I-channel projection energy is evidence of the exact matrix-powering algorithm.
Diameter-filtered synthetic data is available and its correlated graph statistics do not independently cause the result.

techniques.role: Appends each attention result as a new slice so individual polynomial pathways remain algebraically traceable.
Uses identity attention weights so each layer triples the reachable adjacency-power exponent.
Constructs a diameter-3^L+1 counterexample when any intermediate cross-component positive exists.
Bounds information spread to 3^l hops at layer l when no intermediate false positives occur.
Represents each weight block as an I_n algorithm channel plus a J_n global heuristic channel.
Compares cross-component penalties with within-component rewards along nonnegative heuristic directions.
Filters or stratifies training graphs by whether their component diameter exceeds 3^L.
Projects learned weights onto A tensor I and B tensor J and tracks their Frobenius inner-product shares.

evaluations.setting: Two-layer normalized-ReLU standard Transformer on ER(n=20,p=0.08)
evaluations.result: Nearly perfect on held-out ER graphs but nearly zero on same-size two-chain and two-clique OOD graphs.
evaluations.baseline: In-distribution ER holdout versus hand-designed OOD graph families

evaluations.setting: Two- and three-layer Disentangled Transformers on n=24 and n=64 graphs
evaluations.result: At least 99% reliable predictions are reported through distances 3^L, with marked failure beyond that threshold.

evaluations.setting: One-layer Disentangled Transformer on 4,096 ER(n=8,p=0.2) graphs
evaluations.metric: Projected I/J channel energy and equivariance during full-batch gradient descent
evaluations.result: Weights approach the equivariant algebra, with an early rise in both channels followed by increasing I share and decreasing J share.
Filtering to diameter at most 3 promotes the I channel and generalizes best; diameter at most 2 undertrains the at-capacity case, while allowing diameter 4 promotes the heuristic.

evaluations.setting: Stratified mixtures of within- and beyond-capacity graphs
evaluations.metric: 2Chain exact match versus beyond-capacity pair fraction rho
evaluations.result: A small amount of beyond-capacity noise is tolerated while I-channel energy remains dominant, with perfect reported performance around greater than 90% I-channel share; no universal numeric rho threshold is established.
evaluations.baseline: Pure within-capacity and increasingly contaminated mixtures

evaluations.setting: Two-layer standard Transformer trained on one billion n=20 graphs
evaluations.result: Training on ER graphs restricted to diameter at most 9 generalizes substantially better than unrestricted ER training.
evaluations.baseline: The same architecture and optimizer on unfiltered ER data

evaluations.metric: Pair accuracy by distance and equivariance consistency
evaluations.result: The model empirically shows a distance-9 wall and high approximate layerwise equivariance despite signed learned weights.

limitations: The exact expressivity and capacity theorems apply to a nonnegative Disentangled Transformer, not the standard signed-weight model used for headline experiments.
Disentangled width grows exponentially in depth and its ReLU attention/readout differ substantially from ordinary softmax Transformers.
The equivariance theorem assumes arbitrary hidden-state equivariance, a strictly stronger condition than graph-input equivariance.
The population training theory uses projected full-batch gradient descent, special surrogate loss, nonnegativity, regularization, and an invariant parameter algebra absent from AdamW experiments.
The cross-component dominance condition is assumed rather than shown to hold for the reported ER hyperparameters at learned limit points.
Corollary C.22 contains a proof gap: locality after B=0 does not imply successful coverage of all within-capacity pairs.
The approximate-KKT rate conflates a 1/K squared-residual bound with an undefined epsilon-stationarity convention.
Empirical capacity uses 99% pair accuracy, whereas theoretical capacity requires perfection on every graph in a class.
Graph-size generalization is not tested; read-in, read-out, and identity feature dimensions are tied to a fixed n.
OOD evidence is limited mainly to two-chain and two-clique families and cannot identify the learned algorithm uniquely.
Filtering by diameter requires privileged graph computation and changes many graph statistics besides capacity membership.
The standard experiments consume one billion synthetic graphs, with limited reporting of seeds, variance, compute, or confidence intervals.
The paper does not compare against graph neural networks, explicit matrix-powering modules, or curriculum/balancing controls under matched data and compute.
failure_modes: Beyond-capacity connected examples reward dense degree-based predictions because the local channel cannot reach their long paths.
Disconnected dense components such as two cliques expose false positives from the global J channel.
Training only on too-short graphs can fail to teach the at-capacity composition needed for longer paths.
A small change in edge probability can alter connectedness and negative-pair balance, reversing the gradient competition independently of nominal diameter.
Signed weights or softmax normalization can invalidate the nonnegative support-monotonicity arguments.
A model can have high I-channel projection energy yet rely on residual, antisymmetric, or mixed terms for its predictions.
The data lever can select a shortcut that passes the two chosen OOD families without implementing full transitive closure.
Fixed-n node-identity features can prevent length or node-set generalization despite same-size graph-family transfer.
Regularization may suppress the J channel without ensuring that the I channel has learned positive coefficients for every needed adjacency power.
Population-level dynamics may not predict finite-sample AdamW trajectories or minibatch noise.
reusable_insights: Separate constructive expressivity, worst-case capacity, optimization dynamics, and empirical learnability; none implies the next by itself.
Use instance difficulty such as path length or diameter, not only input size, when designing algorithmic curricula.
Include at-capacity examples while limiting unsolvable examples; a curriculum made only of easy cases can underteach composition.
Exploit permutation symmetry to derive interpretable parameter subspaces, but test the exact symmetry assumption and intervene on the channels.
Report graph-level exact match and worst-case families in addition to pair-average accuracy.
Distinguish support containment from support equality; a locality upper bound does not prove algorithm completion.
When claiming data proportions select a mechanism, measure the actual gradient-weighted penalty/reward terms rather than sample counts alone.
Control edge density, component count, degree distribution, diameter, and positive/negative pair balance separately.
Test size extrapolation with size-independent encodings before calling a graph algorithm generalizable.
Compare a learned mechanism against explicit algorithmic and graph-neural baselines under matched supervision and compute.
open_questions: Does the exact 3^L upper bound hold for signed Disentangled weights, normalized softmax attention, multi-head standard Transformers, or residual MLP blocks?
Can one prove sufficient lower bounds on the learned A channel so B=0 actually implies support equality and full capacity?
What observable data statistic guarantees the cross-component dominance inequality during finite-sample training?
Can a curriculum based on local path witnesses avoid computing full graph diameter in advance?
Will capacity-filtered training generalize to larger n with permutation-equivariant, size-independent input/output maps?
Do causal ablations of projected I and J components confirm that those channels, rather than correlated residual weights, determine predictions?
How do graph density, number of components, degree distribution, and diameter independently affect algorithm-versus-heuristic selection?
Can ordinary softmax Transformers learn the same construction with polynomial rather than exponentially growing hidden storage?
How does the prescription compare with explicit transitive-closure networks, recurrent depth, chain-of-thought, and message-passing GNNs under matched compute?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Transformer Reasoning Capabilities via Graph Algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Sanford et al. establish depth/width/token scaling regimes and logarithmic-depth necessity and sufficiency for connectivity across a hierarchy of graph tasks; this paper gives an exact base-3 diameter threshold for a restricted architecture and focuses on data-driven channel selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Struggle to Learn to Search
competitive_landscape.difference: Saparov et al. also find that the right graph distribution lets Transformers learn parallel reachability expansion and that learning degrades with graph size; this paper adds an exact restricted-model capacity theorem and an I/J gradient-decomposition account, but does not test size extrapolation.

competitive_landscape.title: A Little Depth Goes a Long Way: The Expressive Power of Log-Depth Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Merrill and Sabharwal prove highly uniform log-depth Transformers can express connectivity and quantify asymptotic depth scaling; this paper sharpens one simplified model to a nonasymptotic 3^L diameter bound and studies optimization, at the cost of stronger architectural and sign assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Nichani et al. prove gradient descent learns latent causal structure and induction heads in a simplified two-layer model using mutual-information gradients; this paper borrows the disentangling philosophy but targets graph reachability and a competition between local and global equivariant channels.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Transformer Programs
competitive_landscape.difference: Friedman et al. train modified Transformers that can be compiled into discrete programs across algorithmic and NLP tasks; this paper uses appended attention slices for algebraic proofs and weight projections rather than extracting an executable learned connectivity program.

competitive_landscape.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhou et al. connect length generalization to short RASP programs and improve hard tasks such as parity and addition; this paper instead predicts success from diameter-relative capacity and data composition, while evaluating only fixed-n graph-family shifts.

competitive_landscape.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. analyze gradient-flow convergence in a richer two-attention-layer model with softmax-like components, normalization, relative positions, and feed-forward selection on Markov data; this paper obtains graph-specific channel signs and capacity by imposing nonnegativity and an equivariant algebra.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first tight 3^L diameter capacity characterization for an L-layer Disentangled Transformer, a proof that equivariant learned weights split into algorithmic and degree-heuristic channels, a gradient account of how within- versus beyond-capacity data selects those channels, and a capacity-aware data lever that makes standard Transformers learn exact connectivity.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The PDF supplies constructive and upper-bound proofs, block-algebra and projected-gradient appendices, channel-projection diagnostics, diameter-conditioned ER experiments, noise mixtures, and transfer of the filtering intervention to a two-layer standard model on 2Chain and 2Clique.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The exact base-3 restricted-model bound and the graph-specific I/J channel framing are the clearest novel pieces. Log-depth connectivity expressivity, graph-search learnability under suitable data, interpretable modified Transformers, and theoretical gradient learning of algorithmic circuits are strong precedents. The broad headline overstates the formal result: the training theorem needs far more than 'most examples within capacity,' the standard model lies outside the exact theorem, selected OOD success does not identify the exact algorithm, and Appendix C has a concrete gap from B=0 locality to capacity attainment.

reviewer_notes: Read all 33 pages of the official arXiv v2 PDF, including Definitions 3.1-4.6/A.1/C.1/C.14, Theorems 4.3/4.5/4.7/4.9/C.2/C.4/C.5/C.9, Lemmas B.1-B.2 and C.6/C.10-C.18, Corollaries C.20-C.22, equations 1-33, Figures 1-12, and Appendices A-E. The cached PDF SHA-256 exactly matches a fresh stream of https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2510.19753v2 on 2026-08-23. Seven competitor records were checked at exact current official arXiv versions. Confidence is high on the theorem-scope and proof-gap audit; confidence is lower on the learned empirical mechanism because the paper reports projections and selected OOD families without causal channel ablations, exhaustive fixed-n testing, or size generalization.
